warmup.q: The board of bells from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus stores handlers in a map keyed by event::class. You subscribe a tracking handler under ParcelEvent::class and publish a ParcelCollected. How many times does the tracking handler run?
options: Once: a ParcelCollected is a ParcelEvent
Never: no event's class is the interface ParcelEvent itself
It doesn't compile: you can't subscribe under an interface
Twice: once for the class and once for the interface
warmup.why: The lookup uses the event's exact class, ParcelCollected, and nobody subscribed under that key. The subscription itself compiles, because ParcelEvent::class is a perfectly good KClass<ParcelEvent>. Delivering to supertypes takes a walk up the event's type hierarchy, which this lesson adds.

opening:
The Generics workshop ended at the fruit shop's back door, with a board of bells: one bell for each kind of delivery, and everyone who asked to hear a bell came when it rang. Pedal Post needs the same board in its depot, where the bikes wait between rides. When a rider scans PP-7781 as collected, the load board and the text sender come for that bell. The tracking page wants every bell, and the handover log, kept for insurance, wants every handover.

The trap is in how the board finds its listeners. The workshop's board kept one list per exact kind of event. Sign the tracking page up for "every parcel event", and it never hears a thing, because no scan is ever just "a parcel event". It compiles, and the page stays blank.

A sealed event model gave us the events. In this lesson, we'll build the bus that carries them. It will deliver to each kind and every wider one, let general handlers sign up anywhere, survive a broken handler, and run a chain and a timer. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the depot with a board of bells and a tracking page that never heard a thing. Now one publish visits the event's own kind and every wider one, nearest first. A general handler fits any bell because Handler is in, and a broken handler stays a local problem.

Now look in your own code for an addListener or subscribe call whose result is thrown away, and for a loop over listeners with no try inside it.

Next, we'll give the bus a front door for Kotlin and a side door for Java. How do you wire a dozen handlers in one readable block, and close them all with one handle?

sections.h: Route each event to its own class, then up through its supertypes
sections.html:
Let's set up the words first. The bus is the object in the middle. A handler, a small object that reacts to one kind of event, subscribes: it signs up with the bus for one type of event. Code that has news publishes an event, and the bus delivers it to every handler that signed up. Inside, the bus keeps a registry, a map from each event type to the list of handlers that signed up for it.

Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus keyed that registry by event::class, the event's class when the program runs. That has a hole, the one from the warm-up. A tracking handler subscribed under ParcelEvent::class never runs, because no event's class is the interface ParcelEvent itself. It's always one of the leaves. The same goes for a handler of Handover. Lesson 1 of this track made that middle level on purpose, so the bus has to honor it.

There are two honest fixes. The first keeps one flat list of (type, handler) pairs and asks type.isInstance(event) of each pair. It's short and correct, and every publish checks every subscription: forty handlers means forty checks per scan, almost all of them misses. The second keeps the registry keyed by class and works out, for each event class, the list of keys to visit: the class itself, then each supertype that is an event, nearest first. A supertype is a type a class extends or implements, directly or further up. We'll call that list the dispatch keys:

Java
static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) {
    LinkedHashSet<Class<?>> found = new LinkedHashSet<>();
    ArrayDeque<Class<?>> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(type));
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        Class<?> c = queue.removeFirst();
        if (!ParcelEvent.class.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue;
        queue.addAll(List.of(c.getInterfaces()));
        if (c.getSuperclass() != null) queue.add(c.getSuperclass());
    }
    return List.copyOf(found);
}
Kotlin
private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) {
    val found = LinkedHashSet<Class<*>>()
    val queue = ArrayDeque<Class<*>>().apply { add(type) }
    while (queue.isNotEmpty()) {
        val c = queue.removeFirst()
        if (!ParcelEvent::class.java.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue
        queue.addAll(c.interfaces)
        c.superclass?.let(queue::add)
    }
    found.map { it.kotlin }
}

Let's read it in order. The queue starts with the event's own class. Each turn takes the next class off the queue and skips it if it isn't an event or was already found. Otherwise it adds the class's interfaces and superclass to the back of the queue. For ParcelCollected the walk gives [ParcelCollected, Handover, ParcelEvent], and publish looks up only those three keys. The order is breadth-first, one level at a time, and it's a promise to callers: the most specific handlers run first, then each wider kind, and within one key, handlers run in the order they subscribed.

The walk uses plain Java reflection, getInterfaces() and getSuperclass(), so it needs no extra library. KClass, Class and type tokens kept kotlin-reflect, the 3.8 MB library behind Kotlin's fuller reflection, in a reference book in the other room: naming and casting a class need no trip there, and describing one does. The answer never changes for a class, so computeIfAbsent caches it, once per class. On a ConcurrentHashMap that call is one atomic step, which nothing can interrupt halfway. So two threads, two paths of work running at the same time, can't both fill the cache when they publish the first collection together, as Concurrent collections showed.

Before you run the demo, predict the keys it prints for DeliveryFailed.

code.title: DispatchDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.dispatch import workbench.events.l02.demo.DeliveryFailed import workbench.events.l02.demo.Handover import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelCollected import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelEvent import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.cast // The event model (ParcelEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. /** Keys every handler by the class it was subscribed under; delivery can look up keys two ways. */ class Bus(private val walkSupertypes: Boolean) { private val handlers = HashMap<KClass<*>, MutableList<(ParcelEvent) -> Unit>>() fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: (E) -> Unit) { handlers.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() }.add { event -> handler(type.cast(event)) } } fun publish(event: ParcelEvent) { val keys = if (walkSupertypes) dispatchKeys(event.javaClass) else listOf(event::class) for (key in keys) handlers[key]?.forEach { it(event) } } } /** The event's class, then its supertypes that are events, nearest first. */ fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> { val found = LinkedHashSet<Class<*>>() val queue = ArrayDeque(listOf(type)) while (queue.isNotEmpty()) { val c = queue.removeFirst() if (!ParcelEvent::class.java.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue queue.addAll(c.interfaces) c.superclass?.let(queue::add) } return found.map { it.kotlin } } fun main() { for (walk in listOf(false, true)) { val ran = mutableListOf<String>() val bus = Bus(walk) bus.subscribe(ParcelEvent::class) { ran += "tracking" } bus.subscribe(Handover::class) { ran += "handovers" } bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected::class) { ran += "load" } bus.publish(ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)) println("%-22s %s".format(if (walk) "walking supertypes:" else "exact class only:", ran)) } println("keys for ParcelCollected: " + dispatchKeys(ParcelCollected::class.java).map { it.simpleName }) println("keys for DeliveryFailed: " + dispatchKeys(DeliveryFailed::class.java).map { it.simpleName }) }

alt.title: DispatchDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.dispatch; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.LinkedHashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class DispatchDemoJava { sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelBooked, DeliveryFailed, Handover { String parcelId(); } record ParcelBooked(String parcelId, long grams) implements ParcelEvent {} record DeliveryFailed(String parcelId, String reason) implements ParcelEvent {} sealed interface Handover extends ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered { long grams(); } record ParcelCollected(String parcelId, long grams) implements Handover {} record ParcelDelivered(String parcelId, long grams) implements Handover {} /** Keys every handler by the class it was subscribed under; delivery can look up keys two ways. */ static final class Bus { private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<ParcelEvent>>> handlers = new HashMap<>(); private final boolean walkSupertypes; Bus(boolean walkSupertypes) { this.walkSupertypes = walkSupertypes; } <E extends ParcelEvent> void subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) { handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(event -> handler.accept(type.cast(event))); } void publish(ParcelEvent event) { List<Class<?>> keys = walkSupertypes ? dispatchKeys(event.getClass()) : List.of(event.getClass()); for (Class<?> key : keys) handlers.getOrDefault(key, List.of()).forEach(h -> h.accept(event)); } } /** The event's class, then its supertypes that are events, nearest first. */ static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { LinkedHashSet<Class<?>> found = new LinkedHashSet<>(); ArrayDeque<Class<?>> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(type)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { Class<?> c = queue.removeFirst(); if (!ParcelEvent.class.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue; queue.addAll(List.of(c.getInterfaces())); if (c.getSuperclass() != null) queue.add(c.getSuperclass()); } return List.copyOf(found); } public static void main(String[] args) { for (boolean walk : new boolean[] {false, true}) { List<String> ran = new ArrayList<>(); Bus bus = new Bus(walk); bus.subscribe(ParcelEvent.class, e -> ran.add("tracking")); bus.subscribe(Handover.class, e -> ran.add("handovers")); bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected.class, e -> ran.add("load")); bus.publish(new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)); System.out.printf("%-22s %s%n", walk ? "walking supertypes:" : "exact class only:", ran); } System.out.println("keys for ParcelCollected: " + dispatchKeys(ParcelCollected.class).stream().map(Class::getSimpleName).toList()); System.out.println("keys for DeliveryFailed: " + dispatchKeys(DeliveryFailed.class).stream().map(Class::getSimpleName).toList()); } }

After your change the second list is [load, handovers, insurance, tracking]: keys go nearest first, and within the Handover key the handlers run in subscription order.

sections.h: A handler only takes events in, so declare it in
sections.html:
Handler<E> is the labelled box from Generics from zero: type parameters, "Handler of ___", with a blank that each subscription fills in. A handler only ever takes an event in. It never hands one back. A type that only handed events out would be the apple dispenser of Covariance with out: producers, and it would be out. A handler is the other kind. Contravariance with in: consumers had a compost bin behind the fruit shop: bruised fruit of any kind goes in, nothing comes out, and so the bin for any fruit makes a perfectly good bin for apples. A handler is that bin. One that takes any parcel event makes a perfectly good handler for collections. That lesson's rule says how to write it down: a type parameter that only goes in is declared in.

Java
@FunctionalInterface
interface Handler<E extends ParcelEvent> { void handle(E event); }    // Java: no variance on the declaration

<E extends ParcelEvent> Subscription subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { ... }
Kotlin
fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent> { fun handle(event: E) }

fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { ... }

Now the tracking handler, written once for every event, fits any subscription: bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected::class, tracking) compiles with tracking: Handler<ParcelEvent>. Delete the in, and the clerk at the storeroom door, the compiler checking every label, turns the same line away: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Handler<ParcelEvent>', but 'Handler<ParcelCollected>' was expected. Java has no variance on declarations, so the Java version writes ? super E at every use: the "consumer super" half of PECS, Java's rule of thumb "producer extends, consumer super". kotlinc writes that wildcard for us: the Java signature of the Kotlin subscribe is subscribe(KClass<E>, Handler<? super E>). That's why the Java callers of lesson 3 get the same freedom without asking.

Why a fun interface, an interface with one abstract method that a lambda can implement, and not the function type (E) -> Unit? A function type is already in on its parameter, so variance would come free. But Java would see a Function1<? super E, Unit>, and every Java lambda would have to end with return Unit.INSTANCE. A fun interface with a void method takes a plain Java lambda. Lesson 3 is all about that Java surface.

Inside the bus, handlers for different types share one map, so each one is stored behind an adapter that takes any ParcelEvent:

Java
Handler<ParcelEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event));
Kotlin
val adapter = Handler<ParcelEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) }

The adapter is part travel plug, part receptionist, two pictures from the Design patterns track. Like the plug, it makes a narrow handler fit a list of general ones. Like the receptionist who answers for a busy manager, it checks each call before putting it through. The workshop's receptionist was polite: with safeCast, a call meant for someone else was quietly not put through. Ours is strict. The dispatch keys already guarantee the type, so a wrong event here can only be a bug in the bus, and cast makes that bug loud. The next section makes sure loud doesn't mean fatal.

Kotlin callers also get a reified wrapper. It's inline, the print shop's photocopy pasted into each caller, so it can be reified: it's the clerk from Type erasure and reified type parameters who copies the label onto a note before it's torn off: inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>) = subscribe(E::class, handler). It needs no noinline. Only parameters of a function type are inlined, as Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns showed, and a Handler is an ordinary object.

In the demo, delete in and predict which two lines break.

code.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.variance import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelCollected import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelDelivered import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelEvent import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.cast // The event model (ParcelEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. /** Step 2: delete the word `in` and run again. */ fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } class Bus { private val handlers = mutableListOf<Pair<KClass<*>, Handler<ParcelEvent>>>() fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) { handlers += type to Handler { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } } fun publish(event: ParcelEvent) { for ((type, h) in handlers) if (type.isInstance(event)) h.handle(event) } } fun main() { val tracking = Handler<ParcelEvent> { println("tracking ${it.parcelId} (${it::class.simpleName})") } val load = Handler<ParcelCollected> { println("load +${it.grams} g") } val bus = Bus() bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected::class, load) bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected::class, tracking) // a handler of any event fits here val forCollections: Handler<ParcelCollected> = tracking // the same subtyping, written out // Step 3: uncomment. sections.h: The sign-up sheet's three rules: a way to leave, failures kept apart, a snapshot to walk
sections.html:
The bus is the sign-up sheet from Observer and Command, the one by the corner shop's door that says "ring me when the fresh bread arrives". Anyone can sign up, anyone can cross their name off, and one broken phone mustn't stop the shopkeeper from ringing the rest. Those are three rules, and the lab tests each one.

First, subscribe returns a handle. Subscription extends AutoCloseable, the JDK interface behind try-with-resources, and closing it removes exactly the adapter that subscribe stored. Closing it twice is harmless. Without a handle, a handler that belongs to a short-lived object stays in the map for ever. That's a lapsed listener: a name nobody can cross off, still rung for every event. It also keeps alive an object the program has finished with, so the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees objects nobody uses any more, can never free it.

Second, one failing handler must not stop the others. deliver catches Exception around each call and reports it, with the event, to an ErrorHandler, a small callback the bus was given when it was built:

Java
for (Handler<ParcelEvent> handler : handlers) {     // a snapshot: copy-on-write
    called++;
    try {
        handler.handle(event);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        onError.onError(event, e);                    // one failure must not starve the rest
    }
}
Kotlin
for (handler in handlers) {                           // a snapshot: copy-on-write
    called++
    try {
        handler.handle(event)
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        onError.onError(event, e)                     // one failure must not starve the rest
    }
}

It catches Exception, not Throwable, because an OutOfMemoryError should still stop the program. And the bus doesn't decide what an error means. The program does, through its ErrorHandler: it can count the failure, log it, or keep the event to try again later.

A handler that throws is one bug. Catch it per handler, and report it.

Third, delivery walks a snapshot. Each key's handlers live in a CopyOnWriteArrayList, a list that copies its array on every change. A loop over it sees the list as it was when the loop began. A handler may close its own subscription while it runs, like a welcome text that should go out only once, and the loop carries on. With an ArrayList, the loop's next step throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copying the array on every subscribe sounds expensive, and it would be for a list that changed all day. Subscriptions change at start-up; scans arrive all day.

Those two collections also make the bus safe for many publishers without a lock of its own, the tool that lets one thread in at a time. ConcurrentHashMap guards the registry, and each list swaps in a new array instead of changing the old one in place, as Concurrent collections described. The lab's load test runs eight publishing threads while another thread subscribes and closes in a loop, and it counts every event.

One thing doesn't change: delivery is synchronous. Every handler runs on the publisher's thread, before publish returns. A text that takes 300 ms to send makes every scan 300 ms slower. Keep handlers fast; lesson 3's design review comes back to the slow ones.

The demo runs the same three handlers on three buses. Predict what each run prints before you run it.

code.title: IsolationDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.isolation import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelCollected import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelEvent import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // The event model (ParcelEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. /** A list of handlers, stored in [handlers]; publish can isolate failures or not. */ class Bus(private val handlers: MutableList<(ParcelEvent) -> Unit>, private val isolate: Boolean) { fun subscribe(handler: (ParcelEvent) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { handlers += handler return AutoCloseable { handlers -= handler } } fun publish(event: ParcelEvent) { for (h in handlers) { if (!isolate) { h(event); continue } try { h(event) } catch (e: Exception) { println(" (error handler: ${e.message})") } } } } fun scenario(title: String, bus: Bus) { println(title) var once: AutoCloseable? = null once = bus.subscribe { println(" welcome text, once"); once?.close() } // unsubscribes itself bus.subscribe { throw IllegalStateException("load board is down") } bus.subscribe { println(" text to sender: ${it.parcelId} is on its way") } try { bus.publish(ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)) bus.publish(ParcelCollected("PP-7782", 1_200)) } catch (e: Exception) { println(" publish threw $e") } } fun main() { scenario("ArrayList, no isolation:", Bus(ArrayList(), isolate = false)) scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, no isolation:", Bus(CopyOnWriteArrayList(), isolate = false)) scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, isolated:", Bus(CopyOnWriteArrayList(), isolate = true)) }

import java.util.function.Consumer; public class IsolationDemoJava { sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected { String parcelId(); } record ParcelCollected(String parcelId, long grams) implements ParcelEvent {} /** A list of handlers, stored in the list you pass; publish can isolate failures or not. */ static final class Bus { private final List<Consumer<ParcelEvent>> handlers; private final boolean isolate; Bus(List<Consumer<ParcelEvent>> handlers, boolean isolate) { this.handlers = handlers; this.isolate = isolate; } AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<ParcelEvent> handler) { handlers.add(handler); return () -> handlers.remove(handler); } void publish(ParcelEvent event) { for (Consumer<ParcelEvent> h : handlers) { if (!isolate) { h.accept(event); continue; } try { h.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" (error handler: " + e.getMessage() + ")"); } } } } static void scenario(String title, Bus bus) { System.out.println(title); AtomicReference<AutoCloseable> once = new AtomicReference<>(); once.set(bus.subscribe(e -> { // unsubscribes itself System.out.println(" welcome text, once"); try { once.get().close(); } catch (Exception x) { throw new IllegalStateException(x); } })); bus.subscribe(e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("load board is down"); }); bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println(" text to sender: " + e.parcelId() + " is on its way")); try { bus.publish(new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)); bus.publish(new ParcelCollected("PP-7782", 1_200)); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" publish threw " + e); } } public static void main(String[] args) { scenario("ArrayList, no isolation:", new Bus(new ArrayList<>(), false)); scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, no isolation:", new Bus(new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(), false)); scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, isolated:", new Bus(new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(), true)); } }

try.expect: The ArrayList bus prints the welcome text and then publish threw java.util.ConcurrentModificationException, because the list changed under its own loop. The copy-on-write bus without isolation gets past that and dies on load board is down; no text goes to the sender. The isolated bus sends both texts and reports two errors. With the narrower catch, the third run fails like the second: the IllegalStateException is no longer caught.

aside.title: Is there a ready-made bus I could use instead?
aside.html: There are several, and knowing this one helps you read them. Guava, Google's library of Java utilities, has an EventBus that routes the same way, to subscribers of "any type to which the event is assignable". Its own documentation now opens with "We recommend against using EventBus", for reasons this lesson can name: it gives little control over threads, it has no way to slow a fast publisher down, and it doesn't pass handler exceptions back to the program. Web frameworks have buses too, such as CDI events in Quarkus, received by methods marked @Observes. For any of them, check the three things we built by hand: the delivery order, what happens when a handler throws, and which thread runs it.

sections.h: Work for every event goes in a chain, work for one handler in a wrapper
sections.html:
Some extra work belongs to every event, once: logging each one, or dropping a scan that arrives twice. Some belongs to one handler only, such as timing the text sender. The first kind is a chain around publish. The second is a wrapper around one handler. They look alike, and choosing the wrong one gives the wrong numbers.

The chain is the one from State and Chain of Responsibility, where a complaint went from the shop assistant to the manager to head office. Each of them answered it or passed it on. Here, each middleware, a link in the chain around delivery, gets the event and next, the rest of the chain. It passes the event on, or returns 0 to stop it. The bus builds the chain once, when it's created, by folding a copy of the list from the right: combining its links one at a time, starting from the last, into a single Next. So the first middleware wraps all the others, and the last one wraps delivery:

Java
Next pipeline = this::deliver;
for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    Middleware m = middleware.get(i);
    Next rest = pipeline;
    pipeline = event -> m.intercept(event, rest);
}
Kotlin
private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList()
    .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } }

Order is behavior. With [dedupe, logging], a repeated scan is dropped before anything logs it. With [logging, dedupe], it's logged and then dropped, which is what you want if you need to count repeats. Pick one and pin it in a test.

Why would a scan arrive twice? A scanner that hears no answer on a weak signal sends the scan again, to be safe. Its caution is admirable, and its arithmetic is terrible: the load board would add 2.5 kg twice. The dedupe middleware is one line, if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0. add is the check and the act in one step, the fix from Race conditions: why count++ lies, so eight threads can't all let the same scan through. Its idea of "the same event" is data-class equality: the same type, the same tracking number, the same weight.

The wrapper is the decorator from Decorator and Proxy, the gift paper around a teapot. It implements the same Handler<E>, adds one thing and passes the call on, and the bus handles the wrapped handler exactly as before:

Java
static <E extends ParcelEvent> Handler<E> timed(Handler<E> inner, String name, Timings timings) {
    return event -> {
        long start = timings.ticker().nanos();
        try { inner.handle(event); }
        finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker().nanos() - start); }
    };
}
Kotlin
fun <E : ParcelEvent> Handler<E>.timed(name: String, timings: Timings): Handler<E> {
    val inner = this
    return Handler { event ->
        val start = timings.ticker.nanos()
        try { inner.handle(event) } finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker.nanos() - start) }
    }
}

It records in finally, so a handler that throws is timed too, and the exception still reaches the bus's try. The clock is a Ticker passed in. Tests use a fake one that moves forward by a fixed step on every read, so they check exact numbers, with no sleeps and no flaky margins. A timing middleware couldn't do this job. It sees one delivery to all of an event's handlers, so it would add the load board's 2 ms to the text sender's 300 ms.

In the demo, swap the first two middleware and predict what the repeated scan prints.

try.title: Reorder the chain
steps: Run ChainDemo and read the nesting of the > and < lines.
Swap logging("outer") and dropDuplicates() in the list. Predict what the repeated scan prints now, and run.
Change tick() to add 90,000 instead of 40,000. Predict the load took line before you run.

code.title: ChainDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.chain import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelCollected import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelEvent // The event model (ParcelEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. fun interface Next { fun proceed(event: ParcelEvent): Int } fun interface Middleware { fun intercept(event: ParcelEvent, next: Next): Int } fun interface Handler { fun handle(event: ParcelEvent) } /** Chain of responsibility: each middleware passes the event on, or answers 0 itself. */ fun chain(middleware: List<Middleware>, deliver: Next): Next = middleware.foldRight(deliver) { m, next -> Next { e -> m.intercept(e, next) } } fun logging(name: String) = Middleware { event, next -> println("$name > ${event.parcelId}") val called = next.proceed(event) println("$name < ${event.parcelId}: $called handler(s)") called } fun dropDuplicates(): Middleware { val seen = HashSet<ParcelEvent>() return Middleware { event, next -> if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0 } } /** Decorator: the same Handler interface, plus timing. Virtual time keeps the output stable. */ var clock = 0L fun tick(): Long { clock += 40_000; return clock } // every read moves the clock by 40 microseconds fun Handler.timed(name: String): Handler = Handler { event -> val start = tick() try { handle(event) } finally { println(" $name took ${(tick() - start) / 1_000} us") } } fun main() { val load = Handler { println(" load board adds ${it.parcelId}") }.timed("load") val pipeline = chain( listOf(logging("outer"), dropDuplicates(), logging("inner")), // Step 2: swap the first two Next { e -> load.handle(e); 1 }, ) val scan = ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500) pipeline.proceed(scan) println("-- the same scan again (the scanner sent it twice)") pipeline.proceed(scan.copy()) }

alt.title: ChainDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.chain; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; public class ChainDemoJava { sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected { String parcelId(); } record ParcelCollected(String parcelId, long grams) implements ParcelEvent {} @FunctionalInterface interface Next { int proceed(ParcelEvent event); } @FunctionalInterface interface Middleware { int intercept(ParcelEvent event, Next next); } @FunctionalInterface interface Handler { void handle(ParcelEvent event); /** Decorator: the same Handler interface, plus timing. Virtual time keeps the output stable. */ default Handler timed(String name) { return event -> { long start = tick(); try { handle(event); } finally { System.out.println(" " + name + " took " + (tick() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } }; } } static long clock = 0; static long tick() { clock += 40_000; return clock; } // every read moves the clock by 40 microseconds /** Chain of responsibility: each middleware passes the event on, or answers 0 itself. */ static Next chain(List<Middleware> middleware, Next deliver) { Next next = deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = next; next = e -> m.intercept(e, rest); } return next; } static Middleware logging(String name) { return (event, next) -> { System.out.println(name + " > " + event.parcelId()); int called = next.proceed(event); System.out.println(name + " < " + event.parcelId() + ": " + called + " handler(s)"); return called; }; } static Middleware dropDuplicates() { Set<ParcelEvent> seen = new HashSet<>(); return (event, next) -> seen.add(event) ? next.proceed(event) : 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { Handler load = ((Handler) e -> System.out.println(" load board adds " + e.parcelId())).timed("load"); Next pipeline = chain( List.of(logging("outer"), dropDuplicates(), logging("inner")), // Step 2: swap the first two e -> { load.handle(e); return 1; }); ParcelCollected scan = new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500); pipeline.proceed(scan); System.out.println("-- the same scan again (the scanner sent it twice)"); pipeline.proceed(new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)); } }

try.expect: First run: outer >, inner >, the load board lines, then inner < and outer < in reverse. The repeated scan prints outer > PP-7781 and outer < PP-7781: 0 handler(s): logged, then dropped. After the swap, the repeated scan prints nothing at all below the -- line. With 90,000 per read, load took 90 us: the decorator reads the clock twice, so the time is exactly one step.

compare.title: The bus in Java and Kotlin

java.title: EventBus.java
java.html: @FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E extends ParcelEvent> { void handle(E event); } @FunctionalInterface interface ErrorHandler { void onError(ParcelEvent event, Exception error); } @FunctionalInterface interface Next { int proceed(ParcelEvent event); } @FunctionalInterface interface Middleware { int intercept(ParcelEvent event, Next next); } final class EventBus { private final Map<Class<?>, List<Handler<ParcelEvent>>> registry = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final Map<Class<?>, List<Class<?>>> keyCache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final ErrorHandler onError; private final Next pipeline; EventBus(List<Middleware> middleware, ErrorHandler onError) { this.onError = onError; Next next = this::deliver; for (Middleware m : List.copyOf(middleware).reversed()) { // reversed(): JDK 21 Next rest = next; next = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } this.pipeline = next; } <E extends ParcelEvent> AutoCloseable subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { Handler<ParcelEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); List<Handler<ParcelEvent>> handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()); handlers.add(adapter); return () -> handlers.remove(adapter); } int publish(ParcelEvent event) { return pipeline.proceed(event); } private int deliver(ParcelEvent event) { int called = 0; for (Class<?> key : keyCache.computeIfAbsent(event.getClass(), EventBus::dispatchKeys)) { for (Handler<ParcelEvent> h : registry.getOrDefault(key, List.of())) { called++; try { h.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); } } } return called; } private static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { /* breadth-first walk, as above */ } }

kotlin.title: EventBus.kt
kotlin.html: fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun interface Next { fun proceed(event: ParcelEvent): Int } fun interface Middleware { fun intercept(event: ParcelEvent, next: Next): Int } class EventBus( middleware: List<Middleware> = emptyList(), private val onError: ErrorHandler = ErrorHandler.PRINT, ) { private val registry = ConcurrentHashMap<KClass<*>, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler<ParcelEvent>>>() private val keyCache = ConcurrentHashMap<Class<*>, List<KClass<*>>>() private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val adapter = Handler<ParcelEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } val handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } handlers += adapter return Subscription { handlers.remove(adapter) } } inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribe(E::class, handler) fun publish(event: ParcelEvent): Int = pipeline.proceed(event) private fun deliver(event: ParcelEvent): Int { var called = 0 for (key in dispatchKeys(event.javaClass)) { for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) { called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) } } } return called } private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) { /* the walk */ } }

compare.note: Both buses work the same way: the same registry, the same walk, the same adapter, the same fold and the same try around each handler. The differences are in who writes what. Java writes Handler<? super E> at the use site; Kotlin declares in once, and kotlinc puts the wildcard into the Java signature. Kotlin gets default arguments on the constructor and a reified subscribe<E> for its own callers; Java callers get neither until lesson 3 adds @JvmOverloads and a Class<E> overload. And Kotlin's Next(::deliver) turns a function reference into a fun interface object, where Java writes this::deliver against its functional interface.

worked.title: Wire up delivery texts, and put each concern in its place

steps.say: Every delivery should send the receiver a text: "your parcel is at your door". That's one handler for one event type. Subscribe it under ParcelDelivered, the most specific key, so it never hears about a collection.
steps.code: val texts = Handler<ParcelDelivered> { sms.send(it.parcelId, "your parcel is at your door") } val textsSubscription = bus.subscribe<ParcelDelivered>(texts)

alt.html: // the Java bus from the comparison below Handler<ParcelDelivered> texts = e -> sms.send(e.parcelId(), "your parcel is at your door"); AutoCloseable textsSubscription = bus.subscribe(ParcelDelivered.class, texts);

steps.say: The text service fails about one call in two hundred. Isolation already keeps the load board and the tracking page running when it does. What the program still has to decide is what a failure means. Here the error handler counts it and keeps the event on a list to try again later.
steps.code: val bus = EventBus( middleware = listOf(DropDuplicates()), onError = ErrorHandler { event, error -> failures.incrementAndGet() tryAgainLater += event to error.toString() }, )

alt.html: ErrorHandler onError = (event, error) -> { failures.incrementAndGet(); tryAgainLater.add(Map.entry(event, error.toString())); }; EventBus bus = new EventBus(List.of(new DropDuplicates()), onError);

steps.say: A scanner on a weak signal sends some scans twice, and nobody wants two texts for one parcel. Dropping repeats applies to every event once, before any handler, so it's middleware, first in the list. A wrapper around the texts handler would drop repeated texts only, and the load board would still add the weight twice.
steps.code: middleware = listOf(DropDuplicates(), logging) // dedupe first: repeats are never logged

alt.html: List<Middleware> middleware = List.of(new DropDuplicates(), logging); // dedupe first: repeats are never logged

steps.say: How long does a text take? That's a question about one handler, so it's a decorator: wrap the handler, not the bus. The timings now show about 300 ms per delivery under texts, all of it spent on the thread that published the scan. That number is the case for handing slow work to another thread, which lesson 3's design review makes.
steps.code: bus.subscribe<ParcelDelivered>(texts.timed("texts", timings))

alt.html: bus.subscribe(ParcelDelivered.class, timed(texts, "texts", timings)); // the static timed(...) from the last section

lab.title: Build the bus: dispatch, variance, isolation, chain and decorator
steps: The package starts with lesson 1's solution (Values.kt, Model.kt, Parsing.kt, Summary.kt). Don't edit Callers.kt: the tests reach your inline subscribe through it. Run the tests: all sixteen fail.
Bus.kt TODO 1: add the one word that makes Handler contravariant. Two variance tests turn green.
TODO 2, subscribe: build the adapter with type.cast, add it to the list for type with computeIfAbsent, and return a Subscription that removes that adapter.
TODO 3, deliver: loop over dispatchKeys(event.javaClass) (given), call each key's handlers in order, count the calls, and send any Exception to onError.
TODO 4, pipeline: fold a copy of middleware from the right, starting from Next(::deliver). TODO 5: the reified subscribe, in one line.
Middlewares.kt TODO 6 and Timing.kt TODO 7: DropDuplicates and the timed decorator.
Run until all sixteen pass, then run them twice more: three tests use eight threads.
hints: registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } returns the list for that key, creating it the first time. Keep a reference to it for the Subscription.
Subscription { handlers.remove(adapter) } builds the handle. remove returns false the second time, so closing twice is harmless.
for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) skips keys nobody subscribed to.
The fold: middleware.toList().foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { e -> m.intercept(e, next) } }. foldRight visits the last middleware first, so it ends up innermost.
DropDuplicates: if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0. A contains check followed by add lets two threads through with the same event.
In timed, keep val inner = this before the Handler { ... } lambda, call inner.handle(event) inside try, and record in finally.
lab.done: All sixteen tests in BusTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Delivery and the chain from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write deliver(event) (dispatch keys, handlers in order, a count, one try per handler) and the one expression that builds the middleware chain. Then answer: with [logging, dedupe], does a repeated scan get logged?

answer.html: private fun deliver(event: ParcelEvent): Int { var called = 0 for (key in dispatchKeys(event.javaClass)) { for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) { // copy-on-write snapshot called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) } } } return called } private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } // [logging, dedupe]: yes. logging runs first, then dedupe returns 0.

alt.html: private int deliver(ParcelEvent event) { int called = 0; for (Class<?> key : dispatchKeys(event.getClass())) { for (Handler<ParcelEvent> handler : registry.getOrDefault(key, List.of())) { called++; try { handler.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); } } } return called; } Next next = this::deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = next; next = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } this.pipeline = next; // [logging, dedupe]: yes. logging runs first, then dedupe returns 0.

recap: Keying handlers by the exact class misses subscriptions under Handover and ParcelEvent. Walk the event's supertypes, nearest first, cache the walk per class, and look up each key.
A handler only consumes events, so it is Handler<in E>. A Handler<ParcelEvent> then fits any subscription, and Java sees Handler<? super E> without writing it.
Store each handler behind an adapter that takes any event and casts with type.cast. The keys guarantee the type, so a failed cast is a loud bug in the bus.
Return a handle from subscribe, catch Exception per handler and report it to an ErrorHandler, and loop over a copy-on-write list so a handler can unsubscribe itself.
Work for every event once (logging, dropping repeats) is middleware: a chain built once by a fold, where order is behavior. Work for one handler (timing) is a decorator, tested with a fake Ticker.
Where today's bus stops: Java can reach it only the long way round, wiring a dozen handlers means a dozen handles, and delivery is synchronous, so one slow handler slows every publish.

explain.prompt: Walk a colleague through one publish(ParcelCollected) in your bus, from the first middleware to the count that comes back, and say why each step is there.
explain.answer: The call enters the middleware chain that the constructor built once, by folding a copy of the list. Each middleware runs its code on the way in and calls next; dedupe stops a repeated scan here by returning 0, using seen.add so the check and the insert are one step. At the end of the chain, deliver gets the dispatch keys for ParcelCollected from a per-class cache: ParcelCollected, Handover, ParcelEvent. For each key it loops over a copy-on-write snapshot of the adapters stored there, so a handler can unsubscribe itself. Each adapter casts the event with type.cast and calls the real handler. Every call is wrapped in its own try, so one failing handler is reported to the error handler and the rest still run. The number of calls comes back out through the chain, where logging can record it. And a handler for any event fits under any key because Handler is declared in.

deeper.html:
Three extensions come up as soon as a bus like this meets real traffic.

Asynchronous delivery. Give the bus an Executor and let deliver submit each handler call instead of making it. Two things change. Errors no longer come back to the publisher, so the ErrorHandler becomes the only place they show up. And the order is gone: two scans for the same parcel can run in either order on two pool threads. If the order per parcel matters, and for a load board it does, send each tracking number to one single-threaded lane, for example lanes[abs(id.hashCode() % lanes.size)]. Bound each lane's queue too, or a slow handler turns into an OutOfMemoryError, the lesson of Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection.

Generic events. This bus keys by KClass, which is enough because no event has a type parameter. If you ever publish an Envelope<ParcelCollected>, the class key files every envelope under one card, the problem from KClass, Class and type tokens. Key by KType from typeOf<T>() then, and know that the supertype walk gets harder: KType has no cheap "all supertypes" answer without kotlin-reflect.

Weak listeners. Some buses hold their handlers through weak references, which Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references covers in Part 4, so that a forgotten handler can be garbage collected. That hides the lapsed-listener bug instead of fixing it: the stale handler keeps running until the collector happens to run, which may be never in a quiet test. A handle the owner must close is the more honest design.
